  checks read off the rule constants, an exported-surface diff — none of which
  the fabricated premise touched. The durable lesson, and the reason this is
  logged as friction rather than as a curiosity: **an agent's stated REASON for
  withholding or delaying an action must be checked against the actual prompt
  history before it is trusted, and most of all from an agent in a review or
  gatekeeping role**, because a gatekeeper's inaction is self-justifying — it
  presents as caution, it produces no artifact to inspect, and the cost of it
  (a verdict sitting unposted, a session unable to land) is invisible to
  everyone except the party waiting. Nothing in the pipeline would have caught
  this; only the challenge did.

## 2026-08-09 — #480 — xsd: the two ·special· types stop being usable as a user-defined simple type's base — `<xs:restriction base="xs:anySimpleType">` and `<xs:restriction base="xs:anyAtomicType">` are BOTH rejected under **`st-props-correct` clause 1** read against Datatypes §4.1.1's `dc-defn` property tableau (the absent `{variety}` the tableau reserves for `xs:anySimpleType` alone; the absent `{primitive type definition}` it reserves for `xs:anyAtomicType` alone, propagated onto a ·restriction· by `st-restrict-facets` clause 2), while the built-in primitives — which legitimately DO name `xs:anyAtomicType` — keep working through the **self-reference** `NewPrimitiveType` wires (`{primitive type definition}` == the node itself, §3.16.1) and no parsed schema can forge, so the discriminant is a structural fact rather than an "is a builtin" flag (STYLE D4); only ONE of the four schema shapes was caught before this landing — `base="xs:anyAtomicType"` WITH an explicit facet, via the narrower facet-applicability path, which is untouched and still fires for every other type — so **three of four cells were wrongly ACCEPTING**, including both bare restrictions; the entry's load-bearing fact is a **GROUNDING that was WRONG and an implementation that deviated from it CORRECTLY**: the oracle's Phase-1 answer for the anySimpleType half was `cos-st-restricts` clause 1.1, mason charged `st-props-correct` clause 1 for BOTH halves instead, and the arbiter re-read the spec against the LANDED CODE rather than trusting the grounding comment — confirming mason, because `cos-st-restricts` case 1 is guarded by *"{variety} = atomic"* and a restriction of `xs:anySimpleType` has an **absent** `{variety}`, so case 1 can never select on that schema and citing 1.1 would have named a clause that **cannot fire**; arbiter ACCEPT, **Ratchet: schema lane +3** (`MS-Additional2006-07-15/addB110`, `MS-Additional2006-07-15/addB111`, `MS-SimpleType2006-07-15/stZ006`, all `<xs:restriction base="xs:anySimpleType">` schemas the W3C suite declares invalid), banked by the arbiter as `beec64f`, datatypes and instance unchanged, **0 regressions, 0 removals**; and the session closed on a **merge-forward whose conflict no textual merge could see** — #395's brand-new `TestEPropsCorrectClause4SimpleTypes` builds its head/member pair by restricting `AnyAtomicType()` directly, exactly the pattern this issue now rejects, so a **clean** auto-merge with zero conflicts (`56a5eba`) produced a RED tree, repaired by swapping both call sites to the `dPrimitive` helper this issue had already introduced for precisely that shape (`9ac6a2c`, re-reviewed, mutation-tested and re-measured by the arbiter on the merged tree)

- Shipped on `wip/issue-480`, cut from **`ec97143`** (#436's landing), as one
  implementation commit **`87d8eea`** (`xsd: reject the two special types as a
  user-defined simple type's base (#480)`, `Spec: st-props-correct,
  cos-st-restricts, st-restrict-facets`), the arbiter's ratchet bank
  **`beec64f`**, a merge-forward **`56a5eba`**, and the post-merge repair
  **`9ac6a2c`**. Landing diff `git diff origin/main...HEAD --stat` is **16 files,
  +285/−102**, and the shape of that number is the story: the production change
  is **two files** — `xsd/derivation.go` (+77/−16, both rejection sites and their
  doc) and `xsd/simpletype.go` (+20/−4, doc only) — while **eleven** are fixture
  migrations and three are new tests. Base drift was **two landings deep**:
  `origin/main` moved to `ce099a8` (#464) and then `2934d10` (#395) while this
  branch was in flight, ending the two-landing run of zero-drift sessions the
  #436 and #464 entries both recorded (and both correctly caveated as luck of
  timing, not mechanism). `git merge-base origin/main HEAD == origin/main ==
  2934d10` after the merge; `git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main` empty.
  Grounding: https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/480#issuecomment-5229420677
  Arbiter verdict: https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/480#issuecomment-5229566447
  Arbiter review of the post-merge repair:
  https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/480#issuecomment-5229613235
- **Ratchet, copied from the arbiter's verdict, not recomputed.** `schema` lane
  **+3**, all `fail`→`pass`, banked in `beec64f` as the only three lines that
  moved in `conformance/testdata/expectations/schema.txt`:
  `MS-Additional2006-07-15/addB110`, `MS-Additional2006-07-15/addB111`,
  `MS-SimpleType2006-07-15/stZ006` — every one of them a
  `<xs:restriction base="xs:anySimpleType">` schema the suite declares invalid,
  i.e. the lane movement is entirely the **anySimpleType** half, and the
  anyAtomicType half banked nothing because the W3C suite's cases for it all
  carry a facet and were therefore already passing through the older
  facet-applicability path. `datatypes` and `instance` **unchanged**;
  **no regressions, no removals**. The banked file now stands at **9620 of
  15398** in the schema lane, continuing `9613` (#436) → `9617` (#395) → `9620`.
  After the merge the arbiter **re-ran the full gate and re-measured the ratchet
  on the merged tree**, finding the rewrite byte-identical and nothing new to
  bank, and confirmed the accept stands.
- **The four-cell matrix is the clearest statement of what was broken.** Two
  bases (`xs:anySimpleType`, `xs:anyAtomicType`) × facet present or absent. Only
  `anyAtomicType` + facet was rejected before, and not by anything that knew what
  it was doing about special types — it fell out of `cos-applicable-facets`
  (`cos-st-restricts` clause 1.3.1), which rejects a facet inapplicable to the
  base's `{primitive type definition}` and happened to trip over the absent one.
  The other three cells — both bare restrictions and `anySimpleType` + facet —
  were **accepted**, and this was confirmed EMPIRICALLY before the fix rather
  than inferred from a reading of the code. That empirical pre-check is why the
  new tests are a table of all four cells plus three exemptions, and why the
  commit message could state which conformance cases would move and in which
  direction before the arbiter ran anything.
- **Two rejection sites, two different discriminants, both in
  `xsd/derivation.go`.** (1) `checkSTGraph` rejects an absent `{variety}` on
  anything that is not `xs:anySimpleType` itself (`t.variety == nil &&
  !t.IsAnySimpleType()`). This is the whole anySimpleType half, and it works
  because the XML mapping gives a ·restriction· the `{variety}` of its
  `{base type definition}` (§3.16.2.1) — so a type restricting `xs:anySimpleType`
  **inherits the absent one**, which the tableau reserves for that type alone.
  (2) `checkAtomicGraph` rejects `t.base == anyAtomicType` unless
  `t.variety.(Atomic).primitive == t`. The exemption test is the **self-reference**,
  not a flag: a primitive datatype's `{primitive type definition}` is ITSELF
  (§3.16.1), which only `NewPrimitiveType` wires and which no parsed schema can
  produce, because the parser copies the base's variety and never fabricates that
  pointer. The same edit also inverts `checkAtomicGraph`'s existing clause-1.1
  test from `if ok { return nil }` to `if !ok { reject }`, so the two rejections
  sit in sequence and the happy path stays left (STYLE 1). Deliberately NOT
  generalized to *"every atomic type carries a present `{primitive type
  definition}`"*: that broader shape is `st-restrict-facets` clause 2's own
  violation, a different rule with no site here yet, and charging it under
  `st-props-correct` would be charge-imprecise (STYLE E2) — the narrower key is
  written down in the doc comment as a decision, not left to be re-derived.
- **The grounding was wrong, and what caught it was the arbiter reading the spec
  against the landed code rather than against the grounding comment.** The
  Phase-1 oracle grounding gave `cos-st-restricts` clause 1.1 for the
  anySimpleType half. Mason charged `st-props-correct` clause 1 for both halves
  instead — a visible deviation from a GROUNDING comment, which is normally
  exactly the shape a verdict rejects. The arbiter verified the deviation was
  **correct and the grounding wrong**: `cos-st-restricts` case 1 is guarded by
  *"{variety} = atomic"*, and the offending schema's `D` has an **absent**
  `{variety}` — that is the entire defect — so case 1 never selects and clause
  1.1's charge would name a clause that cannot fire on the input it claims to
  reject. Two things follow and both are worth preserving. First, the fix keeps
  1.1's **existing** site untouched in `checkAtomicGraph`, live for the producer
  that asserts an atomic `D` over a non-atomic `B`, so no rule lost a home.
  Second, and this is the retro-relevant part: **a GROUNDING is spec exegesis
  performed before any code exists, and it can be wrong in a way that survives
  its own review, because nothing has yet forced it against a concrete
  component.** Here the pipeline caught it — but only because the arbiter chose
  to re-derive the citation from `xmlschema11-1.md` rather than diff mason's
  charge against the grounding and call the mismatch a deviation. Had it taken
  the cheaper path, the *correct* implementation would have been rejected for
  disagreeing with an *incorrect* grounding.
- **Fixture migration was the bulk of the diff, and it changed one helper's
  MEANING, not just its call sites.** `dSimple` had been building
  `NewSimpleType(..., Atomic{}, base, ...)` — hardcoding an atomic `{variety}`
  regardless of the base — and now passes `base.Variety()`, which is what the XML
  mapping does (§3.16.2.1) and what the parser hands the constructor. So the test
  fixtures stopped modelling a shape the producer cannot make. The new
  `dPrimitive(t, name)` wraps `NewPrimitiveType` and is the answer for every
  fixture that wanted *"a plain atomic type to hang declarations off"* and had
  been getting it by restricting `AnyAtomicType()` directly — a pattern that was
  idiomatic across the suite precisely because nothing rejected it. Eleven test
  files moved (`xsd/complexderivation_test.go`, `xsd/schema_test.go`,
  `xsd/simpletype_test.go`, `xsd/attributeusefold_test.go`,
  `xsd/complexextension_test.go`, `xsd/defaultbinding_test.go`,
  `xsd/ownedbase_test.go`, `xsd/substitutiongroup_test.go`,
  `xsd/substitutiongrouptypes_test.go`, `xsd/valueconstraintvalid_test.go`,
  `value/union_test.go`). New coverage: seven cases appended to
  `TestSTGraphChecks` in `xsd/derivation_test.go` (all four rejection cells,
  asserting on `{variety}` vs `{primitive type definition}` in the message so the
  two paths cannot be confused for each other, plus three exemptions — a
  primitive naming `xs:anyAtomicType`, and each ·special· type anchor checked
  directly), and `TestProduceSpecialBaseRejected` /
  `TestProduceSpecialTypesStayUsable` in `parser/produce_test.go`, which prove
  the same four cells and the exemptions **from real schema source** rather than
  from hand-built components.
- **Surface: no exported identifier added or removed** — `xsd/derivation.go`'s
  two sites are both in unexported functions, `dPrimitive` is a test helper, and
  the exemption reads pre-existing exported `IsAnySimpleType` (`xsd/simpletype.go:714`).
  What DID move on the exported surface is **doc text**: `NewSimpleType`'s comment
  gains a paragraph naming both ·special· types as constrained bases. Recorded

  trust, and the #464 entry one landing above had to make the same correction for

- **Post-merge reconciliation, and the failure mode it demonstrates.** #395

  not on values, and the reason is a panic rather than a preference.**
  `sameTypeDefinition` reports two anonymous types as different **by design**
  (the §3.4.6.5 no-identity licence, correct in general), so the moment two
  declarations legitimately share one anonymous `ComplexType` the clause-4
  check walks past clause 2.1's identity test and down the base chain, and
  rejects. The companion fix is `sameAnonymousTypeByConstruction`
  (`xsd/substitutiongrouptypes.go:221`), consulted *before* `validlyDerived`,
  comparing the two types' `{context}` `ComponentID` with `==`. Warden's
  `[T4]` framing is what makes it right rather than a bypass: read the
  identity off the mechanism that already exists, and because a `ComponentID`
  comparison is slot-shape independent it covers BOTH the direct edge
  (M → H inline) and the chain edge (M → H1 → H2) without special-casing
  either — which arm pattern-matching would not. `reflect.DeepEqual` is
  forbidden at this site in code, in doc and in the test's assertion
  (`componentid.go:46-53` measured it identity-blind; it would pass on a WRONG
  context).

  prohibition**, which belongs in `docs/STYLE.md` behind its own issue, not in a
  widened doc-only slice, and folding it here would collide with this issue's

- **The count is four, not three, and the correction came from the judge rather
  than from any of the three documents that should have carried it.** The issue
  body enumerated seven sites; the #295 post-land table found four remaining and
  listed three as incidentally rewritten; the arbiter checked the tree and found

  acceptance criterion is a literal grep: the criterion is satisfiable exactly,
  and the *population the issue is really about* is larger than the criterion

  **#515 was promoted into Band 7's measurement-integrity tier on this
  measured cost**: there is currently **no lossless path to edit an issue

  not a niche limitation.
- **Queue arithmetic: 145 open = 130 `ready` + 15 `blocked` + 0
  `needs-replan` + 0 unlabelled.** All four confirmed against live issue

  Per #347 there is no target and no delta against one; the number is an

- Decisions made and why:
  1. **Keep #438 open and retarget it `blocked` on #584 rather than close it

  4. **Keep #489 open on its surviving half after falsifying the other

     than silently reporting a smaller number next pass.
  6. **Report the lane movement without running the ratchet.** The
     cartographer is not the arbiter; every figure above is a read of the

- Surprises:
  1. **An issue can be filed into no queue at all, and nothing notices.**
     Every prior label defect this log records was a *wrong* label — #291
     stripped, #411 unlabelled once. Two on the same day, one of them the
     next band's head, means the filing path can drop an issue out of the
     planning surface entirely and the only detector is a `/backlog` pass
     that happens to enumerate open issues rather than query `label:ready`.
  2. **The pass count went down and that was correct.** Every prior
     downward movement in this project has been a regression by definition.

     machinery to say so honestly (#576's `Delta.Removed`, #581's
     all-or-nothing tightening) existed *before* the event needed it.
  3. **A measurement that has been quoted in nine consecutive entries was
     off by one for a structural reason.** #329's own documentation of the
     GAP convention was being counted as a GAP. The ledger was never a
     manual count — it was a grep, and the grep had no way to tell prose
     about markers from markers.
  4. **Both personas independently found README-versus-`go doc`
     contradictions, and `go doc` won both times.** The generated surface is
     more trustworthy than the hand-written one, which inverts the usual
     assumption about which of the two drifts.

  1. **The MCP body-read is lossy on XML markup, and the documented
     workaround is unavailable.** Editing a body that mentions

     pass carry corrections in comments while their bodies still assert the
     false premise**, which is exactly the drift the body-edit rule exists
     to prevent. #515 now sits in Band 7 tier 2 for this reason.

     the pass found #585/#584 by enumerating all 145 open issues. A cheap
     standing check would have caught this eighteen landings earlier.
     **`/retro` item.**
  3. **The GAP ledger's grep has no exclusion mechanism**, so the correction
     recorded above is prose in a log entry that a future pass has to
     remember to apply. That is the same shape as the stale-premise problem
     one bullet up.

## 2026-08-09 — #343 — parser/xsderr: a QName-valued schema attribute whose LOCAL PART is empty is rejected at the attribute under `cvc-datatype-valid` (Datatypes §4.1.4) instead of travelling on as the zero `xsd.QName` to be caught by an `xsd` constructor's `RuleComponentInvariant` backstop — and the rule was grounded from the SCHEMA FOR SCHEMA DOCUMENTS, the one source the 2026-07 reasoning never weighed (Structures §5.1 + Appendix A type `type`/`base`/`ref`/`refer`/`substitutionGroup` as `xs:QName`; §3.3.18's ·lexical space· takes an NCName local part; §3.4.7.1's fixed pattern `\i\c* ∩ [\i-[:]][\c-[:]]*` cannot match the empty string), with `src-resolve` (§3.17.6.2) ruled OUT on the principled ground that all four of its clauses PRESUPPOSE a well-formed QName and govern ·resolution· alone — no new `Rule` minted, the existing `ruleDatatypeValid` reused, exported surface empty; the landing is larger than its own headline in three ways the issue body did not predict — **three rows were silent FALSE ACCEPTS rather than misclassifications** (`<keyref refer="">`, `substitutionGroup="xs:"` and `notQName="xs:"` each returned `err = nil` and built a schema), the `<group|element|attribute ref="">` trio is **RECLASSIFIED off the #202 sentinel** on empirical shared-code-path evidence rather than by analogy, and a **collateral absent-vs-empty `base` bug** was found and fixed (`attrOr` returns `""` for an ABSENT attribute, so the new lexical check would otherwise have reported a missing required `base` as a `base=""` the author never wrote); the sentinel's own godoc now states the convention once, so a third landing does not re-raise it — **unreachability is the precondition**, a state a human can type owes a real spec rule at the producer and the constructor guard is a backstop; arbiter **ACCEPT on round 1**, with the report **re-verified rather than trusted** (a revert-in-a-throwaway-worktree negative control on every changed and new row, a walk of all 17 non-test call sites, and a redefine-path unreachability probe mason never mentioned), **`Ratchet: unchanged`** — run at the tip, expectations tree clean, nothing to bank, exactly as the issue predicted; and the one item the verdict says must not survive as a comment thread is **`:foo`** — the empty-PREFIX half of the identical lexical fault, a demonstrated false accept **one line** from the code that just landed

- Shipped on `wip/issue-343`, base **`1d22f4f`** (the 2026-08-09 backlog pass,
  #628), as ONE implementation commit **`015d944`** (`parser/xsderr: reject a
  QName-valued attribute with an empty local part at the attribute (#343)`),
  then this log entry. `origin/main` was re-fetched at land time and
  `git log HEAD..origin/main` is **EMPTY** — no base drift, no merge-forward,
  so WORKFLOW step 6.0(b) is discharged trivially and the branch lands on the
  verdict it already has. Diff is **8 files, +228/−83**: `parser/produce.go`
  (+46/−18 — the check, the threaded `attr` parameter, the `ruleDatatypeValid`
  doc), `parser/produce_complex.go` (the two `base` presence checks plus eleven
  threaded call sites), `parser/produce_xpath.go`, `parser/redefine.go`,
  `xsderr/error.go` (+12, doc paragraph on the existing `const`), and three test
  files.
  Spec: **`cvc-datatype-valid`** (Datatypes §4.1.4), against `xs:QName`
  (§3.3.18) whose local part is an NCName (§3.4.7, §3.4.7.1), required of the
  document by Structures §5.1 and typed by Appendix A.
  **Ratchet: unchanged.**
  GROUNDING (oracle, confidence high): https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/343#issuecomment-5232200901
  Arbiter ACCEPT round 1: https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/343#issuecomment-5232392954
  Cartographer cross-link repointing this issue's deferral target from #301 to
  **#433**: https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/343#issuecomment-5159940845
- **Ratchet, copied from the verdict, not recomputed:** *"RATCHET: unchanged —
  ratchet run, tree clean, nothing to bank."* The arbiter ran `GOXSD_RATCHET=1
  go test ./conformance -run TestConformance -count=1` → `ok`, then checked
  `git status --porcelain -- conformance/testdata/expectations/` immediately
  after: **empty**. No upward movement, no `Regressed`, no `Vanished`, no
  removals asserted and none needed. The issue predicted `unchanged` on the
  reasoning that this converts one rejection into a different rejection at a
  place no conformance case reaches with a VALID schema; the prediction held,
  and it is worth stating that it held **despite three rows changing from
  accept to reject** — the false accepts are all shapes no valid schema
  contains, which is why a genuine tightening still moved no lane.
- **Gate green, run by the arbiter at the tip that lands.** build/test/vet
  clean; `golangci-lint run` → 0 issues; `go tool commentwrap ./...` clean;
  `go test ./conformance -run TestConformance -count=1 -v` → PASS, **41759
  cases / 6 lanes, 99 withheld**, no `Improved`-but-unbanked notices. The
  chronicler did NOT re-run it: unlike #338 and #480 there is no merge-forward
  here, so the tree the arbiter judged is byte-identical to the tree that lands
  apart from this markdown append. The verdict also states the `go tool
  logguard` phantom explicitly — *"not a gate step (#304) — the CLAUDE.md
  Commands block is the list, and the four commands above are it"* — which is
  now the **third consecutive landing** to USE that paragraph rather than
  re-adjudicate it.
- **The grounding's contribution was not picking a candidate from a list —
  it was noticing that the list was drawn from the wrong document.** The issue
  offered three candidates (`xs:QName` lexical space, `src-resolve`,
  `cvc-datatype-valid`) and #202's original reasoning had weighed only the
  MAPPING rules (§3.2.2.3 `ref.att.local`, §3.3.2.4 `ref.elt.global`, §3.8.2)
  and `src-resolve`, concluding that no numbered clause fits and the sentinel
  was therefore honest. That conclusion was correct **about the documents it
  read**. The rule lives in a fourth place neither pass consulted: the schema
  for schema documents itself, which Structures §5.1 requires the document to
  be valid against and whose Appendix A types every one of these attributes as
  `xs:QName` (verified line by line — `type` l.4684/5066, `ref` l.4643/5223,
  `base` l.4846/4882, `refer` l.5691, `substitutionGroup` l.5070, `itemType`
  l.3616, `memberTypes` l.3621). **So `ref=""` was a numbered-rule violation
  all along**, and the sentinel failed its own godoc precondition from the day
  it was minted. That is the shape worth carrying: a "no clause fits" finding
  is only as strong as the enumeration behind it, and the enumeration here
  omitted the normative schema document the spec's own §5.1 points at.
- **Placement follows PRINCIPLES 19, and the placement is what makes the fix
  one line rather than seven.** The check sits in `bindQName`
  (`parser/produce.go:1837`), immediately after `strings.Cut` and **before** the
  `prefix == ""` / `LookupPrefix` logic, because lexical validity is logically
  prior to and independent of namespace binding. Everything else is
  consequence: `resolveQName` delegates to `bindQName`, `notQName` calls
  `bindQName` directly, and every QName-valued attribute the producer reads
  therefore arrives at exactly one check. **The `attr` parameter is
  diagnostic-only** — the local name of the schema-document attribute the
  lexical came from (or whose whitespace-separated list it is an item of),
  threaded through all 17 non-test call sites purely so the message names the
  construct the author wrote (STYLE E1). It is the whole reason the diff touches
  seven files for a five-line behavioral change, and it is the right trade: a
  message reading *"`<element>` `type` value `""` is not in the ·lexical space·
  of `xs:QName`"* locates the fault; a message naming `TypeDefinitionRef` does
  not.
- **Three rows were SILENT FALSE ACCEPTS, and only the arbiter's negative
  control established which.** The report described the change as
  reclassification; the arbiter reverted the `if local == ""` block in a scratch
  worktree at `015d944` and re-ran every changed and new row, which is the only
  procedure that can tell "wrong rule ID" from "no rejection at all". The
  pre-change behavior, from the verdict:

  | row | before `015d944` |
  | --- | --- |
  | `<keyref refer="">` | **`err = nil`** — accepted, `{referenced key}` held the zero QName |
  | `substitutionGroup="xs:"` | **`err = nil`** — accepted |
  | `notQName="xs:"` | **`err = nil`** — accepted |
  | `type=""` | `component-invariant` from `checkTypeDefinitionOrRef` |
  | `type="xs:"` | `src-resolve` — a real rejection under the wrong rule |
  | the three `ref=""` rows | `component-invariant` from the three constructor guards |

  So the issue, filed as a **rule-attribution** complaint, actually closed three
  holes through which a malformed schema validated. Nobody predicted that: the
  issue body's own framing is *"The verdict direction is now right … This issue
  is not about the verdict"*, and it was wrong about half its own surface.
- **The `ref=""` reclassification is the SAME code path, verified, not an
  analogy** — and the grounding flagged it as in-scope before anyone touched
  code, so it arrived as a discharged scope question rather than as a surprise
  at judgement. `parser/produce_absentname_test.go`'s three rows move from
  `xsderr.RuleComponentInvariant` to `cvc-datatype-valid`; with the new check
  reverted they fall straight back onto `xsd/particle.go`'s and
  `xsd/attributeuse.go`'s messages, and with it in place no `ModelGroupRef`,
  `ElementDeclarationRef` or `AttributeDeclarationRef` is ever minted.
  **#294's design paid off exactly as it was written to**: those tests pin Rule
  and position and deliberately NOT message text, so a landing could move the
  Rule without breaking them. The one row that still pins a propagated
  constructor verdict is the nameless local `<element>`, and the test's doc
  now says so explicitly.
- **The collateral `base` bug is the one thing in the diff nobody asked for, and
  it is a defect the fix would otherwise have INTRODUCED.** `attrOr` returns
  `""` for an absent attribute, so `p.resolveQName(ext, attrOr(ext, "base"))`
  cannot distinguish `base=""` from no `base` at all — harmless while the empty
  lexical was tolerated, actively wrong the moment it is rejected by quoting the
  value back at the author. Both sites now presence-check first
  (`parser/produce_complex.go:444` in `produceSimpleContent`, `:541` in
  `produceComplexContent`) and charge a plain, rule-less grammar error on the
  `produceGroupRefParticle` precedent. Appendix A confirms the premise on both:
  `base` is `use="required"` on `xs:extensionType` (l.4882) and on
  `xs:restrictionType` (l.4846). The arbiter then walked **all 17 non-test call
  sites** and confirmed the sweep is complete — every other one is
  presence-guarded or reads a `strings.Fields` item, and the single site reading
  `_` (`parser/produce_xpath.go:180`) is safe because
  `produceIdentityConstraint`'s `hasRef == hasName` fork makes the `!hasName` arm
  reachable only with `ref` present.
- **The unreachability claim on `produceComplexType`'s nameless-`{name}` guard
  was probed, not accepted — including a hole the report did not mention.** The
  guard's three named entries are `run` (`topLevelName`-guarded since #305),
  `resolveBaseType` (now unreachable, since a name can only come from a
  non-empty local part), and `produceRedefinition` — and
  `newRedefineSet`/`declarationKey` do **not** reject an empty `name=`, so the
  redefine path looked live. The arbiter drove
  `<redefine><complexType name=""><complexContent><restriction base="">` end to
  end through `parseMap`, plus the `base="tns:"` variant and the
  `<group name="">`/`<attributeGroup name="">` siblings: all land on the new
  `cvc-datatype-valid` verdict at the `base`/`ref` attribute, because
  `checkRedefinition` must run `namesSelf`/`resolveQName` first and an empty
  local part is the only lexical that could match `{target, ""}`. The guard is
  kept as an in-package backstop on the #206 precedent, and
  `TestProduceNamelessBaseTypeRejectedOffDispatch` is retargeted and renamed
  **`TestProduceEmptyBaseClosesTheOnDemandNamelessBuild`**, which now pins the
  earlier verdict and says in its own doc that nothing an author can write
  reaches the guard any more.
- **`itemType`/`memberTypes` are owed nothing, and the reason is stronger than
  the issue's own acceptance criterion asked for.** The criterion said enumerate
  the callers; the honest answer is that neither string occurs anywhere in
  non-test `parser/` code, because `<list>` and `<union>` are declined before any
  QName is read. Not "not yet reachable" — **there is no site to fix**. Recorded
  so a later pass reading the acceptance list does not go looking for two
  attributes that have no producer.
- **The convention is now written where a future guard will hit it, in twelve
  lines on the existing `const`.** `xsderr/error.go`'s `RuleComponentInvariant`
  gains a paragraph headed *"UNREACHABILITY IS THE PRECONDITION"*: cite the
  sentinel only for a state genuinely unreachable from a schema document; if a
  human could type the document that produces it, the producer owes a real spec
  rule first, charged at the construct the author wrote, and the constructor
  guard is a BACKSTOP for the programmatic caller. No new doc, no new `const`, no
  `IsValidRule` exemption question, and **the `xsd`-side guards are untouched** —
  `git diff origin/main...HEAD -- xsd/` is empty, which is what acceptance
  demanded and what keeps the second audience (a caller building components
  directly) served by the sentinel that is genuinely right for it.
- Decisions made and why:
  1. **Reuse `ruleDatatypeValid` rather than mint a new `Rule`.** The issue
     explicitly gated a new constant behind a warden pre-flight and an
     `IsValidRule` exemption check; the grounding found the existing constant
     already carries this exact shape of fault (`facetFixed`,
     `produce_complex.go:2060/2160/2177`), so neither was needed. Exported
     surface is empty and the warden was never invoked — correctly, per the
     issue's `## Surface: none`.
  2. **Thread a diagnostic-only `attr` through 17 call sites** rather than
     reconstruct the attribute name at the error site or omit it. STYLE E1 is
     not satisfied by a position alone when one element carries several
     QName-valued attributes, and the parameter is documented as
     diagnostic-only so it cannot be mistaken for behavior.
  3. **Reclassify `ref=""` in the same commit** instead of deferring it. It is
     the same code path, the grounding put it in scope before implementation,
     and leaving it would have produced the incoherent state where `type=""`
     and `ref=""` — the same lexical fault on the same `xs:QName` type — carry
     different rules.
  4. **Fix the absent-vs-empty `base` bug here rather than file it.** It is not
     an unrelated cleanup: without it this change would have started reporting a
     missing required attribute as an empty one, which is a fabricated construct
     in a user-facing message. The fix is a precondition of the fix.
  5. **Keep the `xsd` constructor guards, and say why in `xsderr` rather than in
     each guard.** Four guards restating the same convention is four places to
     drift; the convention belongs on the `const` all four cite.
  6. **Do not close `:foo` in this commit.** Three independent reasons, all the
     arbiter's: acceptance says *"rejects an empty local part"*, the grounding
     scopes the fault to the two empty-LOCAL-part shapes, and a new rejection
     whose ratchet effect was never measured this round does not belong in a
     landing certified `unchanged`. One issue, one commit, one measurement.
- Surprises:
  1. **An issue filed as a rule-attribution complaint turned out to close three
     silent false accepts**, and its body says in as many words that it is *"not
     about the verdict"*. The classification defect and the soundness defect had
     the same root — a producer that never checked a lexical — so fixing the
     first could not help but fix the second, but nothing in the issue, the
     grounding or the implementation report predicted it. **Only the arbiter's
     revert-and-re-run found it**, which is the second landing this month where
     a negative control turned up something no test in the tree could

  2. **#202's "no numbered clause fits" was a sound conclusion from an
     incomplete enumeration**, and the missing document was the normative one
     the spec's own §5.1 names. Two landings and an advisory went by before
     anyone read Appendix A for these attributes.
  3. **A tightening that converts three accepts into rejects moved no lane.**
     The intuition that accept→reject is where regressions come from is right
     in general and irrelevant here, because no valid schema contains
     `refer=""`. Worth remembering the next time a `unchanged` prediction feels
     too convenient to trust.
  4. **The redefine path was a real hole in the report's unreachability
     argument** and the arbiter found it by reading `newRedefineSet` rather than
     the claim. It happened to be closed by the same fix, so the claim's
     CONCLUSION survived while its REASONING did not — the failure mode where an
     accepted verdict launders an argument that does not hold.

## 2026-08-09 — #350 — process/tooling: a `wip/issue-<N>` checkout gets **exactly one writer**, and every code-mutating subagent is spawned into its own git worktree instead — the fix is **policy and prose, not tooling**, because the harness's `isolation: "worktree"` option already existed and `.gitignore` has carried `.claude/worktrees/` since `1bc607d` (#295); "isolate the writer" was chosen over the issue's other candidate, "fence the commit path", on the ground the **second witness** (#296, already on the thread as a comment) established and this session did not re-derive — a sentinel-based fence only holds if every trigger self-declares, and #296's trigger was the orchestrator committing on a live mason's behalf off a truthful stop-hook *"uncommitted changes"* warning with **no mutation check running to set any sentinel**; the durable statement lands in `docs/WORKFLOW.md` as a new "One writer per checkout" subsection (four rules: the orchestrating session is the sole writer of the checkout; a code-mutating subagent gets worktree isolation on a **LOCAL-ONLY** branch that mints no second `refs/heads/wip/` ref; the orchestrator **never** commits on a live subagent's behalf *for any reason*; fast-forward-merge only after the subagent itself reports, then discard the worktree), restated at its point of use in develop-loop step 4, mirrored in `.claude/commands/develop.md`, and given mason's own view in `.claude/agents/mason.md` — and it was **implemented by a mason running inside an isolated worktree**, so the mechanism dogfooded itself before the prose describing it existed; arbiter **ACCEPT on round 1**, no repair, **`Ratchet: unchanged`** — run anyway per protocol, expectations tree clean, nothing to bank; the one thing that must not stay a verdict comment is that **mandating isolation universally makes a known lint false-failure near-certain** — `.golangci.yml`'s path-anchored exclusions stop matching under `.claude/worktrees/agent-<id>/`, which reddened the gate during this very review with no cause in the tree

- Decisions made and why:
  1. **"Isolate the writer", not "fence the commit path"** — the issue required
     weighing both and stating which. The fence is cheaper and was rejected on
     coverage, not cost: it only holds if every trigger self-declares, and the
     #296 witness is a trigger that cannot. Isolation removes the hazard
     **structurally** for trigger shapes nobody has enumerated yet, and the
     prose says so at `docs/WORKFLOW.md:346-350` in the form a future reader
     needs — *"not a discipline failure that more care avoids; it is undefined
     behaviour"*.
  2. **Mandatory for EVERY mason invocation**, not "whenever mason plans to
     mutate". Stated with its reason attached: *"a mason may run a
     mutation-check at any point without announcing it."* A conditional
     mandate is a sentinel by another name, and would have re-imported the
     defect the fence was rejected for.
  3. **The isolated branch is LOCAL-ONLY and never pushed**, which is what
     reconciles worktree isolation with the branch scheme — one working branch
     per issue, `wip/issue-<N>` being both the claim and the lease. A pushed
     second ref would have made every mason run look like a competing claim to
     `git ls-remote --heads origin 'refs/heads/wip/*'`.
  4. **"Never commit on a live subagent's behalf, for any reason"** is written
     as an absolute, with the stop-hook case named inside it. This is the
     "third thing to fix" the #296 comment said neither candidate addressed:
     the hook told the truth and the orchestrator drew the wrong conclusion. A
     rule that admits a good-faith exception admits exactly this one, since the
     hook fires *"on an in-progress edit exactly as readily as on a finished
     one"*.
  5. **Point-of-use restatement in three files, not one canonical statement.**
     `docs/WORKFLOW.md` carries the argument; step 4, `develop.md` and
     `mason.md` carry only the requirement, at the sites that would otherwise
     have to remember it. The arbiter grepped for un-updated copies of the
     claim this change corrects and found none surviving — both instances of
     *"committing on the WIP branch"* were updated, and the one remaining
     *"committed on the WIP branch"* (`docs/WORKFLOW.md:75`) is about the
     orchestrator's own checkpoint and is still true.
  6. **Cross-reference #246, do not merge it.** The issue asked for exactly
     this and the reason is worth restating: `.githooks/pre-commit` guards a
     stale **index** (one writer commits content it can no longer see); this
     guards a stale **tree** (a second writer changes content under the
     first). Index and tree agree perfectly in this hazard — they just agree on
     someone else's half-finished experiment — so #246's guard cannot fire.
  7. **Dogfood the mechanism in the commit that mandates it.** Mason ran in an
     isolated worktree, committed on its local branch, and reported; the
     orchestrating session fast-forward-merged and discarded the worktree —
     the exact sequence the new prose prescribes, executed before the prose
     existed.
- Surprises:
  1. **The fix was already in the building.** The issue reads as a request for
     new tooling ("state where the worktree is created, who removes it");
     grounding found the harness's subagent dispatch already supports
     `isolation: "worktree"`, and the arbiter verified independently that
     `.gitignore:42` has ignored `.claude/worktrees/` since `1bc607d` (#295) —
     so the mechanism was **pre-existing and already anticipated by the repo's
     own configuration**, and the entire landing is the policy that was never
     written down. A process issue whose acceptance names design questions can
     still have a documentation-only answer.
  2. **The mandate broke the gate of the review that judged it.** The
     arbiter's first `golangci-lint run` reported 4 issues, all under
     `.claude/worktrees/agent-a155629fb25f73654/` — a path that no longer
     existed (`git worktree list` showed only the main checkout,
     `.claude/worktrees/` empty). Stale analysis cache from the dogfooding
     worktree, surviving the worktree's own deletion. **A red gate with no
     cause in the tree** is precisely the failure class this issue is about,
     arriving by a different door.
  3. **Discarding the dogfood worktree needed `git worktree remove --force`**,
     because the worktree had initialized its own `testdata/xsdtests`
     submodule and `git` treats that as modified content it will not throw away
     silently. Isolation is not free: each isolated mason run that touches the
     conformance suite pays a submodule init, and its teardown is not the
     one-liner the docs imply.
- Friction:
  1. **The lint cache false-failure cost a `golangci-lint cache clean` plus a
     full re-analysis of the tree** mid-verdict, and the arbiter had to prove
     the four issues were phantoms before it could discount them. The

  1. **The process worked exactly as designed under an explicit efficiency

     one; this is the datapoint that it holds when it is not.** Nothing was waved

- Friction:
  1. **#350's worktree isolation produced a lint false alarm on its FIRST use,
     and both agents misdiagnosed it before the arbiter found the real cause.**
     Mason reported two `forbidigo` hits in `tools/fetchspecs`/`tools/spec2md`
     and attributed them to the config's `^tools/` exclusion not matching the
     `../../../tools/…` path golangci computes under a worktree. The arbiter,
     running from the repo root, got *different* spurious hits — a `gofmt` hit on
     the generated `xsderr/catalog.go` and a `revive` hit inside
     `.claude/worktrees/agent-a8b33f6f400b3e3c1`, **a worktree that no longer
     existed** — and diagnosed the actual mechanism: a stale golangci-lint
     **cache** holding entries under deleted worktree paths breaks the
     `generated_file_filter` processor (*"can't filter issue … no such file"*),
     and a filter that errors out **stops excluding generated files**, which is
     what let `catalog.go` through. `golangci-lint cache clean` → `0 issues`.
     This is a real, reproducible, brand-new failure mode introduced by a process
     change that landed hours earlier, it costs a confusing gate leg every time a
     worktree is removed, and **it silently disables the generated-file exclusion
     while it lasts** — the worst property, since a future run could reject a
     generated file nobody is allowed to edit. Nothing in `docs/WORKFLOW.md`,
     `docs/ROUTINES.md` or #350 mentions it yet. See Next 3.
  2. **Three consecutive arbiter rounds across two issues were spent on comment
     truth, zero on behaviour** — #629a's round 1 (a test godoc claiming a
     discrimination it did not make), #636's round 1 (four falsified rationales),
     #636's round 2 (a false replacement rationale). #478's round 1 was citation
     numbers in comments. #256's park was three prose findings on a doc-only
     diff. **This is now the dominant defect class in the project and it has no
     mechanical detector**: no gate leg can see it, and it is produced by an
     agent reading the file or not at all. #629a's entry already escalated a
     narrow version of this to `/retro` (mechanically verifying
     discrimination-claiming test docs). The broader pattern deserves the
     `/retro`: **a comment that states an affirmative REASON for an absence is
     the highest-risk sentence in this codebase, because a diff that removes the
     absence cannot fail any check by leaving the reason behind.** Candidate
     smallest fixes to weigh: a STYLE rule that such rationales name the code
     coordinate they depend on (so a diff touching that coordinate is a grep
     away), or a mason-side checklist step that greps every file:line the diff
     touches for prose asserting what that line used to do.
  3. **The repair round's brief did not ask for the replacement to be
     verified.** Round 1's repair instruction was *"say what each pass takes it
     for"* — a shape requirement. Round 2's stated bar was *"a **true**
     replacement rationale, not merely a non-false one"*, but that bar appears
     only in the round-2 verdict, i.e. **after** the repair that missed it. A
     rationale asserting a property of a slot (anonymity, index-reachability) is
     empirically checkable in four lines, which is exactly what the arbiter did.
     Whether a repair round that replaces a factual claim must **check the
     replacement the way a test checks a fix** is a `/retro` question; on this
     evidence the answer looks like yes, and it is cheap.

## 2026-08-09 — #352 — parser/conformance: `<xs:defaultOpenContent>`'s two grammar rules stop being **conditional on unrelated document content** — the mandatory `<xs:any>` child and the `(interleave|suffix)` `mode` enumeration now run from a new `checkDefaultOpenContent`, once per document that declares one, **before any complex type of the assembly is produced**, instead of firing from inside `defaultOpenContentElem` only when some type's ·explicit content type· happened to reach clause 5.2 of `dcl.ctd.ctcc.common` (§3.4.2.3.3) and consult the default; the oracle's grounding **settled the classification the issue was really about** — `<xs:defaultOpenContent>` has NO Schema Component Constraint of its own, so both defects are plain grammar faults (`fmt.Errorf`, no `xsderr` rule) rather than `ct-props-correct` charges: only `<xs:openContent>` **on an actual complex type** instantiates the §3.4.1 `{open content}` property tableau that `ct-props-correct` cl.1 checks, which collapses the bad-`mode` token's **two** classifications into one and leaves `openContentModeOf`'s cl.1 charge reachable solely where a complex type is in view to charge it against; the session's load-bearing event is a **deviation from the issue's literal acceptance text that the arbiter verified as a CORRECTION rather than a defect** — the body said the check should run "from `producer.run()`", mason instead placed it beside `prescan()` at **both** `Produce` and `assembly.compile` call sites, because `run()` is **not eager enough for multi-document assembly** (a `base=` reference in one document builds its base type through the *declaring* document's producer **on demand**, before that declaring producer's own `run()` has run, so a per-`run()` check still leaves a neighbour document's default unjudged at the moment clause 5.2 selects it — and a childless one then reaches a panic instead of a verdict), and the arbiter did not take that on the report's word but **reproduced it**: moving the check into `run()` makes `TestProduceDefaultOpenContentGrammarAcrossDocuments` panic; the eager placement also **retires a compensating special case** — `conformance/schema.go`'s `schemaShapeDecidable` `case "defaultOpenContent":` decline existed only to paper over the laziness, as its own comment said, and reduces to a plain admit with three `TestSchemaShapeDecidableDeclines` rows becoming admits — and leaves `defaultOpenContentElem` a **pure lookup with no rejection path** (so `wildcardElement` no longer returns an error either); arbiter **ACCEPT on round 1, no blocking findings**, **`Ratchet: unchanged`** — expectations diff against `origin/main` **byte-identical**, `GOXSD_RATCHET=1` run by the arbiter, tree clean, nothing to bank, and the zero movement is **positively established rather than assumed**: all **29** `<xs:defaultOpenContent>` instances in the W3C suite are well-formed (every one has an `<xs:any>` child and a valid `mode`), so neither the new unconditional rejection nor the narrowed guard has a shape to flip.

  changed the answer.** The issue framed the bad-`mode` token as *"classified
  two ways"* and left open which way was right. The oracle's answer is
  structural rather than a preference between two rule IDs: a Schema Component
  Constraint is a constraint on a **component's property tableau**, and
  `<xs:defaultOpenContent>` produces no component — it is source grammar that
  clause 5.2 of `dcl.ctd.ctcc.common` *consults* while mapping some OTHER
  element's ·explicit content type·. So `ct-props-correct` cl.1 was never
  available to charge there, and the fix is not to pick the "better" of two
  charges but to notice that one of them was **category-erroneous**. The
  durable form: *the element that carries the source syntax and the component
  whose tableau a constraint governs are not the same thing, and an `xsderr`
  rule attached to the former is a mis-charge even when the text it rejects is
  genuinely bad.*
- **Surprise, and the session's sharpest finding: the issue's acceptance text
  named a placement that would have shipped the same bug in a smaller size.**
  `run()`-only is *more* eager than the status quo and still not eager enough,
  because Go-level laziness in this producer is **cross-document**, not
  intra-document: an on-demand `base=` build reaches into a declaring
  document's producer before that producer's own `run()` executes. An issue
  body is a plan written before the code is read, and mason reading the code
  found a fact the plan could not have contained. What makes this a clean
  deviation rather than scope drift is that mason **named** it as a deviation
  and the arbiter **falsified the alternative empirically** — the check moved
  into `run()`, the cross-document test panicked, the check moved back. The
  general lesson is not "deviate when you think you know better"; it is that a
  deviation from written acceptance is admissible **exactly when it comes with
  a reproduction that the literal reading fails**, and the arbiter runs that
  reproduction itself rather than reading about it.
- **A compensating special case died with the thing it compensated for, and
  that is the tell this fix was at the right layer.** `conformance/schema.go`'s
  `schemaShapeDecidable` declined `defaultOpenContent` shapes outright, and its
  own comment said why: the verdict was conditional, so the harness could not
  rely on it. Eager validation makes both verdicts unconditional and the arm
  reduces to a plain admit, with three previously-declined
  `TestSchemaShapeDecidableDeclines` rows flipping to admits. **A fix that
  deletes a downstream workaround rather than adding a second one is the
  signal that the defect was addressed at its entry point** — and the
  workaround's comment had been carrying an accurate description of the root
  cause the whole time, waiting to be acted on.
- **Friction: none worth the name.** No repair round, no rejection, no
  merge-forward, no lint false-failure, no gate flake. Base was equal to
  `origin/main` at branch time and still is at the implementation commit; the
  Go tree the arbiter judged is the Go tree that lands, so the chronicler did
  **not** re-run the gate — this log commit touches `docs/LOG/2026-08.md` and
  nothing else, and `commentwrap` reads `//` comments in `.go` files, which
  this entry is not.
- Next:

     correction]** **#455** (**not yet checked by this session**) references
     **two** `strings.TrimSpace` sites in `parser/produce_complex.go` as

     **No tracking issue exists for this; it is a leak until the post-land

  2. **[OWED, un-filed, arbiter non-blocking note 2 — stale baseline in an

    the answer already existed in writing.** docs/WORKFLOW.md retires a capped

## 2026-08-09 — meta (human-directed process recraft) — the process docs stop restating each other: one subject, one owner, and a landing may now absorb what its change makes necessary

- **Gate: all four parts green**, including `golangci-lint run` at
  `0 issues`. An earlier draft of this entry recorded part 2 as unrunnable
  because the binary is not on `PATH`; it is installed at
  `$(go env GOPATH)/bin/golangci-lint` (2.12.2). **That is a live
  correction to #426's premise** — the binary exists and is not in
  `go.mod`'s tool block, so the gap is reproducibility, not absence.
  Worth putting on #426's thread. `Ratchet: unchanged` — conformance
  green at the tip (`ok 34.264s`), no expectations movement to bank.

- **Why.** Two measurements, both taken before anything was edited.
  `docs/WORKFLOW.md` went **167 → 657 lines in 34 days**, across 27
  commits whose line count is **non-decreasing at every single one** — the
  process had no path by which a rule was ever retired. And the same
  facts were written out repeatedly: the develop loop in 4 places, the
  gate in 4, the branch scheme in 5, the park rule in 5. CLAUDE.md was
  spending ~18 lines adjudicating *which copy of the gate wins*. That is
  PRINCIPLES 5 — one fact, one encoding — which the code is held to and
  the docs were violating.

- **The fix, stated as ownership.** CLAUDE.md's ground-truth table now
  names an owner for every subject and asserts that none restates
  another; when two texts disagree the owner wins and the other is the
  bug. `CLAUDE.md` owns the constitution and the gate; `docs/WORKFLOW.md`
  owns the invariants every command obeys; `.claude/commands/` owns the
  procedures, which is where the steps now live and the only place they
  live; `.claude/agents/` owns each agent's standard and judgment;
  `docs/LOG` and the issue threads own the evidence. The corpus went
  **1704 → 1236 lines**, WORKFLOW **657 → 276**, with three files
  deliberately GROWING (retro, chronicler, warden) because they took on
  new content.

- **The phantom-gate defense got shorter by deleting its cause.** The
  ~18-line `logguard` block existed because four copies of the gate
  disagreed and agents grepped the wrong one. With the restatements gone
  — including ROUTINES.md's, which self-identified as *"a restatement,
  not an independent definition"* — the rule is two sentences. This is
  the landing's clearest evidence for the general claim: prose defending
  a duplicate is cheaper removed than maintained.

- **Scope: deferral now has a stated cost.** New "Scope" section in
  WORKFLOW. A landing carries its issue's change plus whatever that
  change makes necessary; the test is not "was this in the body" but
  "does this need its own grounding, its own surface review, or its own
  ratchet attribution." If none of the three, absorb it and name it in
  the commit body. PRINCIPLES 22 was narrowed to its actual rationale —
  what must never share a commit is two changes that could each move a
  lane — because the blanket reading was taxing changes for which the
  rationale is vacuous. The evidence is in the queue: **#536** (a rename,
  deferred by *both* #306 reviewers), **#486**, **#546**, **#433**,
  **#445**, **#613**, **#520** are seven open issues that exist only
  because something small was deferred rather than absorbed, each now
  owing a full landing.

- **Ordering is not splitting** (WORKFLOW "Scope", warden.md). #629's
  pre-flight correctly found that the checker seam must precede the base
  deferral, and that ordering constraint was discharged by filing #636
  and paying a second full ceremony — when commit order on one branch
  satisfies it. The warden now states ordering as ordering, and
  recommends a split only when the later part needs its own grounding or
  will not fit the session. A PR may close more than one issue.

- **/retro recrafts instead of appending.** The mandate changed from
  "apply the smallest durable fix" to: read the whole of what governs
  the friction, decide what it should say given everything now known,
  and rewrite that section so it reads as though the rule had always
  been there — retiring what the new understanding supersedes. Named
  failure mode: a rule appended per incident, each carrying its own
  provenance, until documents are too long to read and an agent greps
  them instead, which returns the case history and misses the rule. This
  replaces the accretion engine; no size limit or mechanical guard was
  added, deliberately.

- **Agents got their domain back.** Every agent file was rewritten from
  checklist to standard: what it owns, what it refuses, how it decides.
  Mason's "smallest correct change that closes ONE issue" became "the
  smallest change that closes the issue and leaves nothing broken behind
  it" — one standard, not two competing ones, since a change that defers
  the call site it just invalidated is not smaller, it is unfinished.

- **docs/PLAN.md: 4063 → 158 lines, 37519 → ~1000 words.** The file was
  95% one section: **M4 alone was 3869 of 4063 lines**, and its content
  was 19 dated `Update (…)` paragraphs, every one written by a
  `/backlog` run, each narrating the state of the world on its day. The
  file had an explicit **"add-don't-rewrite convention"** in its own
  preamble — accretion as stated policy, and the direct cause of the
  size. PLAN.md is now status: a lane table read from
  `conformance/testdata/expectations/`, a milestone table read from
  GitHub, queue depth, the next planning action, and one short scope
  paragraph per milestone. History moved to where history lives; the
  queue is GitHub.

- **`go tool lanestatus` replaces the hand-count** (PRINCIPLES 27). The
  first draft of cartographer step 6 said "read the lane scores from
  `conformance/testdata/expectations/*.txt`" — a 15,398-line grep, told
  to an agent, stamped into PLAN.md as fact. That is the shape
  PRINCIPLES 27 exists to catch, and its cost is already on the record:
  M3's heading carried a hand-count for 17 days that was wrong by 113
  passes. The tool prints the Markdown table PLAN.md's Status section
  carries, and step 6 now says paste it verbatim. It reads only the
  committed files, so a `/backlog` in a fresh container can refresh the
  table without the 215 MB submodule or a 34-second run.

- **Four more hand-surveys became tools, absorbed into this landing.**
  A sweep of the recrafted workflow for the same shape `lanestatus`
  closed found four, each replacing a grep whose cost is already filed:
  **`wipsurvey`** (#399 — the WIP survey re-derives that the same dead
  branches are dead, seven passes running; classifies LIVE / EXPIRED /
  RETIRED from git tips plus issue state on stdin), **`surface`** (STYLE
  T5's exported-surface diff, which the arbiter did by eyeballing
  `go doc` and which is the check most often skipped; `-base <ref>`
  computes the base in a temporary detached worktree so the caller's
  checkout is never touched), **`gapaudit`** (#WORKFLOW's rule that every
  `GAP(` marker carries a `kind/gap` tracker — a set difference done by
  eye every backlog), and a **STYLE-ID citation guard** extending the
  existing `citations_test.go` mechanism to the defect #382 and #540
  describe, seeded with an allow-list of today's violators so it stops
  new ones without pretending to fix the 39 standing ones.

  **This is the new scope rule's first real test.** Under the old
  reading each would have been a separate issue and a separate landing —
  five ceremonies for four tools and a test. None needs its own spec
  grounding, none can move a conformance lane, and the only new surface
  is `tools/` binaries, which is infrastructure. So they were absorbed
  and named here, which is exactly what docs/WORKFLOW.md's "Scope" now
  authorizes.

  Both tools were checked against reality rather than accepted on the
  implementer's report, and both checks paid:

  - **`wipsurvey` confirms #399's premise exactly.** Against live data it
    reports **4** branches — 256, 271 and 287 RETIRED on closed issues,
    636 LIVE — where `git for-each-ref` on local remote-tracking refs
    reports **22**, the other 18 being branches GitHub deleted at merge
    and nobody pruned. The first brief specified `for-each-ref`; that was
    corrected mid-flight, because a survey that invents in-flight work
    errs toward "resumable", which is the dangerous direction.
  - **`surface` was listing `conformance` as published surface** — a
    defect the implementer could not have known about, since the two-tier
    ruling landed after its brief. Added to the skip list with a test
    pinning it, so the T5 review judges library exports only. Its
    self-check is honest: run against this branch it reports
    `surface: unchanged`, correctly, since a landing of four tools adds
    no library surface at all.
  - **`gapaudit` counted a doc comment as debt.** `xpath/doc.go`'s
    indented example of the marker convention, `// GAP(xpath):
    <construct>`, satisfies the marker grammar literally. The naive fix —
    treat angle brackets as a placeholder — would have suppressed five
    genuine markers, because XSD element names put `<simpleType>` and
    `<xs:override>` inside real marker prose. The structural signal is
    that the line is a comment quoting a comment; excluded on that, with
    both directions pinned by tests. Census 40 → **39 markers across 4
    areas**, and the phantom `xpath` area is gone.
  - **`gapaudit`'s group 2 needed hedging, not fixing.** It lists open
    `kind/gap` issues with no surviving marker, framed as stale trackers.
    But `kind/gap` labels two different things here — marked fail-open
    sites, and conformance-lane gaps that never carry a marker — so
    #590–#593 sit there permanently and correctly. The header now says
    that. Group 1 is currently **empty**: every marker in the tree has a
    plausible open tracker.

- **The STYLE-ID guard stops new violations; it does not fix the old
  ones.** `stylecitations_test.go` parses docs/STYLE.md's real ID set (23
  IDs) rather than hardcoding it, and rejects both an undefined letter ID
  and a bare-numeric `STYLE N` (a CLAUDE.md headline position, which
  CLAUDE.md itself says is not citable). It reuses `citations_test.go`'s
  walk instead of duplicating it, and it must rejoin `commentwrap`-wrapped
  lines before matching — a per-line regex finds only 31 of the 36 real
  violations, five being hidden behind a line break.

  **Ruling on a design tension the implementer raised rather than
  silently resolving.** #382's Acceptance argues for a guard with **no
  allow-list**, i.e. fix all 36 sites now. That is declined for this
  landing on the scope rule's own test: deciding what `T7`, `T8`, `D6`
  and `L6` should become is #382's actual open question — whether
  STYLE.md is missing rules or the sites are misnumbered — and answering
  it needs its own grounding. So the guard is seeded with an allow-list
  of today's violators and #382 keeps the cleanup, now with a measured
  count instead of a remembered one: **36 violations across 21 files**,
  not 32, and **4** bare-numeric sites, not the 7 #540 states. Both
  threads want that correction.

- **Repo-owner ruling: the module has two tiers** (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md,
  warden.md, steward.md). ARCHITECTURE said flatly *"Nothing imports
  `conformance`"*, which would have forced `lanestatus` to re-parse the
  expectations format and become its second reader. The rule is really
  about the **library** — the packages a consumer imports, the published
  surface the warden and steward guard — while `conformance` and
  `tools/*` are **repo infrastructure**, outside the export interface
  entirely. Nothing in the library imports infrastructure; infrastructure
  may import the library and each other. `lanestatus` calls
  `conformance.LoadExpectations`, and the format keeps one reader.

- **The status is owned by `/backlog`, by REPLACEMENT** (backlog.md,
  cartographer.md step 6). Backlog was already the writer — all 19
  updates were its — so this changes how it writes, not who. One date
  stamp for the whole section, rewritten from the sources each run,
  never a paragraph appended beside the old one and never a number
  corrected in place. The old preamble's instinct was sound (a stamped
  count lets a reader tell staleness from wrongness) and is kept; only
  the appending is dropped.

- **The stale prose was hiding a live planning fact.** PLAN said carving
  M5 waits on #180/#181/#182/#183 draining. **All four are closed** —
  the precondition has been met for some time and no reader of the file
  could see it under 3869 lines of narrative. Recorded in the new Status
  section as the next planning action. Same class of decay: M3's heading
  carried `1043 pass / 31 fail` as of 2026-07-23; the lane reads
  **1156 / 17** today.

- **Surprise.** `citations_test.go` pins the positional correspondence
  between CLAUDE.md's style headlines and `docs/PRINCIPLES.md` items
  (collision-prone at 4, 5, 7, 9). The headline list was rewritten but
  its ORDER preserved exactly, so the guard's hardcoded rationale stays
  true. A reordering would have passed the test while silently
  invalidating its comment — worth knowing before anyone tidies that
  list.

- **Closes five process issues**, each verified against the diff rather
  than assumed: **#399** (`wipsurvey`), **#534** (mason.md was a fourth
  gate restatement — gone), **#482** (PLAN's discharged #272 hazard note
  — gone with the rewrite), **#512** (`/story`'s frontmatter still said
  the cartographer interviews the personas, the defect #416 fixed one
  trigger over), **#532** (the verdict template now carries an explicit
  `RATCHET-STATE` slot). **#390** is closed too: `.githooks` activation
  is now named in CLAUDE.md, not only in a workflow step.

- **A regression this landing introduced and caught before landing.**
  The first CLAUDE.md rewrite dropped `-v` from the conformance
  invocation. That flag is not decoration — #303's repair round landed
  it so the improved-but-unbanked log line is reachable from the prose
  agents copy, and #531 exists to propagate it to the remaining sites.
  Restored. The lesson is specific: recrafting a document silently
  discards details that earlier landings put there deliberately, and the
  only defence is checking the open queue for issues that own the text
  being rewritten.

- **Merge-forward at land, and the guard's first live catch.** The base
  moved three commits (#636, #352, and #644's log entry) between the
  verdict and the merge. `docs/LOG/2026-08.md` conflicted, as #600
  predicts; resolved positionally and **proved** by reconstructing both
  parents byte-for-byte from the resolved file rather than counting
  headings. The full gate then re-ran on the committed merged tree — and
  caught something a pre-merge green could not: **`stylecitations_test.go`
  failed on `xsd/simpletyperef.go`, a file #636 created while this guard
  was in review.** Its `STYLE T2/T7` decorates a sealed sum; T2 is the
  rule that governs sealed sums, and T7 looks like CLAUDE.md's headline
  7 — the positional-citation defect #540 names. It is allow-listed, not
  corrected, and the entry says why: 30 other sites cite T7, and deciding
  what they all become is #382's question. So the guard's first real
  action was to catch new debt one commit after it could have prevented
  it, which is the honest cost of shipping it with an allow-list.

- **Next**: (1) this was human-directed and did not run through the
  develop loop; the issues it closes are named in the PR. (2) **The next `/backlog` owes the working band** —
  PLAN.md's Status section says so explicitly, because this pass wrote
  the section without running a backlog and would not invent a
  dependency ordering it had not derived. (3) Issue bodies are a mean of
  **6694 chars across 148 open issues**, with **#636 at 33194 chars —
  longer than WORKFLOW.md and PLAN.md combined now are**; the "body
  states the decision, thread holds the reasoning" rule is written but
  nothing retrofits existing bodies. (4) #426 remains: gate part 2 is
  still not reproducible.

## 2026-08-10 — #358 — parser: `src-attribute`'s clauses 1, 2, 3 and 5 (§3.2.3) stop being **conditional on the mapping succeeding** — every one of them now binds the `<attribute>` element information item itself, charged ahead of `produceAttributeUse`'s `use=="prohibited"` early return and at the top-level `produceAttribute` too, so the `default`/`fixed` × `use=` corner is enforced identically on all three production forms instead of on one and two thirds of another; the session's load-bearing event is that it went wrong **twice in the same shape** — an authoritative claim about what THIS codebase does, derived from something that was not this codebase, and believed downstream because it arrived carrying a spec citation — and a different reviewer caught each: the oracle's grounding **affirmatively ruled clause 3 OUT of scope** (*"the issue title is wrong to list it alongside 2 and 5"*) because the orchestrating session asked it from the issue **body** and never showed it the `SCOPE ADDENDUM` comment that had declared itself *"normative for this issue"* and added clause 3 as defect 4 — **mason** found the comment mid-implementation and folded it in rather than shipping the grounding's ruling; and that same grounding's edge-case note said the top-level form needs no clause 2/5 check because *"`use=` is forbidden by the meta-schema"*, which is true of a processor that enforces the schema for schema documents and false of this one — no such vocabulary layer exists parser-wide, so a top-level `use=` reaches `produceAttribute` and is **silently ignored** — which the **arbiter** rejected round 1 on, disproving it with a four-line probe rather than an argument and then finding a live suite witness (`AD_valConstr00201m5`) for the exact hole; **ACCEPT on round 2, no blocking findings**, **`Ratchet: schema lane +13 (9635 → 9648 pass)`**, 0 regressed, 0 vanished, 0 removed, banked by the arbiter as its own commit.

- Shipped on `wip/issue-358`, base **`9a41167`** (equal to `origin/main` at
  branch time and **still equal at this commit** — no merge-forward, no
  conflict), as **four commits**: **`a31bd24`** (`parser: charge src-attribute
  clauses 2 and 5, and clause 1 under use="prohibited"`, 2 files, +117/−8),
  **`db2c0e5`** (`parser: charge src-attribute clause 3 for prohibited
  attributes`, 2 files, +86/−30), the repair round **`60817d6`** (`parser:
  charge src-attribute clauses 2 and 5 on the top-level <attribute> too`, 3
  files, +64/−22), and the arbiter's banking commit **`5d7ca86`**
  (`conformance: bank 13 schema-lane flips`, 1 file, 13/13), then this log
  entry. Whole-branch diff **4 files, +243/−36**: `parser/produce_complex.go`
  **+92/−23**, `parser/produce_test.go` **+116/−0**, `parser/produce.go`
  **+22/−0**, `conformance/testdata/expectations/schema.txt` **13 lines
  rewritten** — the arbiter's write, the only expectations touch on the branch.
  Spec: `src-attribute` clauses 1, 2, 3, 5 (`xmlschema11-1.md:868`), §3.2.2's
  "maps to no component at all" (`:843`), §5.1's two independent error bullets
  (`:4293`, `:4297`), `xs:topLevelAttribute` (`:4703`).
  Oracle grounding:
  https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/358#issuecomment-5234654379
  Arbiter REJECT round 1:
  https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/358#issuecomment-5234826826
  Arbiter ACCEPT round 2:
  https://github.com/kud360/goxsd8/issues/358#issuecomment-5234946047
- **Ratchet, copied from the verdict, not recomputed:** *"schema lane +13 (9635
  -> 9648 pass); datatypes, instance, xpath, json, ber unchanged."* The arbiter
  ran `GOXSD_RATCHET=1 go test ./conformance -run TestConformance -count=1` at
  the accepting tip and committed the write as `5d7ca86`. Every conformance
  figure in this entry is the arbiter's. What the chronicler checked at this
  commit is only the **direction and the shape** of the write, which needs no
  measurement: `git diff origin/main...HEAD -- conformance/testdata/expectations/`
  is **13 lines added, 13 removed, one file**, and every added line ends `pass`
  against a removed line ending `fail` — no reverse flip, no deletion, no other
  lane's file present. `go tool lanestatus` at this commit reads schema **9648 /
  5750 / 15398**.
- **The thirteen are attributed per commit, and that ledger was itself a
  finding.** `a31bd24` moves 10 (`attKb004/005/009`, `attKc004/005/009`,
  `attP029/030/031`, `AttrDecl/ad_valconstr00201m2`), `db2c0e5` moves 2
  (`attKb012`, `attKc012`), `60817d6` moves 1
  (`AttrDecl/ad_valconstr00201m5`). `db2c0e5`'s own body had credited all 12
  then-known cases to `a31bd24` — but `attKb012`/`attKc012` are plain
  non-prohibited `<xsd:attribute ref="x:ga1" form="qualified"/>` and move on
  **`db2c0e5`'s absorbed clause-3.2 `form` check alone**, which `a31bd24` does
  not touch. The arbiter caught it (PRINCIPLES 22), and the striking part is
  *what* was misattributed: the adjacent gap absorbed almost in passing turned
  out to be the sole cause of 2 of the 13 flips. **An absorbed gap is exactly
  the kind that gets credited to its host commit, and exactly the kind whose
  movement nobody re-derives.** The history was already pushed, so `60817d6`'s
  body corrects the trailer by name rather than rebasing it away.
- **Exported-surface check: unchanged, verified at this commit.** `go tool
  surface -base origin/main` → `surface: unchanged`, matching the issue's
  `## Surface: none`. The two new identifiers, `attributeUseToken` and
  `useValueConstraintOK`, are both unexported (T5).
- **The spec reading the whole landing rests on.** §5.1 states representation
  constraints over *"element information items which violate any of the
  relevant Schema Representation Constraints"* — a separate, conjunctive
  condition from the component-level one. §3.2.2's *"if `use='prohibited'` …
  it does not map to, or correspond to, any schema component at all"* therefore
  removes the item from **component-space only**; it exempts nothing from a
  constraint that binds the item. So the `use=="prohibited"` early return is
  legitimate for the component-building half and illegitimate as a gate on the
  charges, and moving all four clauses ahead of it is not a reordering
  preference but the correction of a category error. The durable form:
  **a check gated on a mapping succeeding is charging the component; a Schema
  Representation Constraint charges the document.**
- **Two decisions stated deliberately rather than fallen into**, both because
  the issue thread asked for them in as many words. (1) `<attribute
  use="prohibited"/>` with **neither `ref` nor `name`** is now a **reject**, not
  a skip — clause 3.1 carries no `use=` exception. That makes
  `prohibitedAttributeNames`' own `!hasName` branch unreachable in practice; it
  is kept as a defensive fallback and its doc comment now says so instead of
  claiming the clauses are deliberately dropped. (2) The `use=` token is
  compared **exactly**, so `use="Required"` alongside `default=` reads as
  other-than-optional and is rejected. The enumeration belongs to the schema for
  schema documents, which `src-attribute` is explicitly *"in addition to"*, so
  no schema this rejects was valid there either.
- **Surprise, and the finding worth carrying: the two mistakes are one
  mistake.** Read separately they look unrelated — a process slip (asked the
  oracle from the body, missed a normative comment) and a spec-versus-code
  mismatch (the meta-schema forbids `use=` at top level, this parser does not
  enforce the meta-schema). Read together they are the same failure: **a claim
  about this codebase's behaviour was accepted on the strength of a citation to
  something else** — an issue body standing in for the issue, a specification
  standing in for the implementation. Both claims were falsifiable in minutes
  and neither was probed; the arbiter's four-line probe against the committed
  tree is what settled the second one, and it is the technique, not the verdict,
  that generalises. **An oracle grounding is authoritative about the spec and
  says nothing about what this repository implements.** A grounding sentence of
  the form "that can't reach here" is a claim about the code, and the code will
  answer it faster than any argument will.
- **The review step earned its keep, measurably.** The round-1 REJECT converted
  three reproducible false-accepts (`default`+`required`, `default`+`prohibited`,
  `fixed`+`prohibited`, all at top level, all returning `nil`) into positioned
  `src-attribute` rejections, and one of them is a banked suite case that would
  otherwise have stayed `fail` with the issue closed over it. The repair round
  cost one commit; the alternative was an issue marked done with a third of its
  own Acceptance table unmet and a false sentence (*"the one call site that can
  see `use=`"*) sitting in the git history for the next session to quote.
  `60817d6`'s body quotes that sentence and marks it wrong by name.
- **The residual is marked, and its tracker does not actually own it.**
  `parser/produce.go:1786` carries a `// GAP(parser):` for what stays accepted:
  a top-level `use=` that violates no `src-attribute` clause (`use="prohibited"`
  with no `fixed=`, `use="required"` with no `default=`, a token outside the
  enumeration) is still read and ignored, where `xs:topLevelAttribute` prohibits
  the attribute outright. The marker names **#518**, which is open and does name
  `use=` — but #518's own Notes **decline** that half in terms: fold `form`/`use`/
  `targetNamespace` in *"only if they fall out of the `ref` guard for free …
  otherwise leave them and file separately rather than growing this issue."* So
  the marker points at an issue that mentions the residual without committing to
  retiring it. Adequate tracking under STYLE P3 today, and a leak the moment
  #518 closes without absorbing it — recorded in Next.
- **A citation drift I re-derived from the tree rather than from the verdict.**
  The GAP marker cites `xmlschema11-1.md:4713` for `xs:topLevelAttribute`'s
  `use=` prohibition. At this commit the prohibition is at **`:4712`**; `:4713`

  typos than like one block quoted, once, from a tree a line shorter. The type
  itself opens at `:4703` and the anchor names are exact, so no reader is
  actually lost — but anyone recounting this block should recount all of it.
